title: From a program to a container and a running service
summary: Follow application code from a folder on a laptop to a replaceable running instance. Learn process, image, container, virtual machine, and Pod before seeing a deployment diagram.
objectives: Distinguish source code, a built image, and a running container.
Explain how a container differs from a typical virtual machine.
Trace a cautious application deployment without assuming packaging solves data durability.

terms.definition: A running instance of a program, with execution state and memory managed by the operating system.
A packaged filesystem and runtime metadata used to start containers.
A running workload with operating-system isolation and resource controls; it is not a separate physical computer.
A virtualized computer environment that typically runs its own guest operating-system kernel.
A service that stores and distributes container images.
Kubernetes’s smallest deployable workload unit, containing one or more closely related containers sharing selected resources.
In Kubernetes, a workload resource and controller arrangement for managing desired replicas and updates of suitable applications.

retrieval: Why should saved notes not depend on one application process’s memory?
What does the reverse proxy do when an instance is not ready?

sections.title: First understand what is running
sections.markdown:
You have a folder containing the Pocket Notes server code. The folder is not yet a running service. Starting the program creates a process. That process executes instructions, uses memory, opens files, and listens for requests through the operating system. If you start the same program twice with suitable configuration, you can have two processes with separate memory.

This explains a common confusion: two copies of the same code do not automatically share the same data. If instance A stores a note only in a local variable, instance B does not acquire it just because both came from the same folder. They need a shared durable data design when the product requires shared saved notes.

Processes also depend on their environment. A program may require a particular language runtime, installed libraries, operating-system features, certificates, or configuration. “It worked on my laptop” can mean the laptop happened to contain something the next machine lacks. Packaging addresses part of that problem.

sections.title: An image is a package, not a running service
sections.markdown:
An image is the packaged starting point for a workload: application files, a suitable runtime, dependencies, and startup metadata. Building it does not start a server.

| Thing | Example | Does it contain the new note Maya saves tomorrow? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | notes-api code at revision r12 | No; it describes behavior |
| Image | Built artifact identified by a digest | No; it is the tested starting package |
| Container | Instance A started from that image | Only if the process receives or stores it |
| Durable database | Saved note n61 | Yes, after a successful commit under its contract |

Think of one prepared recipe kit producing several cooking sessions. Each session has its own work in progress. Several containers from one image likewise have separate process state.

A registry stores images for machines to fetch. A digest identifies exact artifact content; a tag such as latest can be moved to different content. Record which digest was tested and deployed, and use compatible runtime environments. Packaging reduces environment surprises; it does not prove application correctness or supply live user data.

sections.title: A container changes the process’s environment
sections.markdown:
A container runtime starts processes using isolation and resource-control mechanisms. In a typical Linux container arrangement, containers share the host's kernel while receiving separated views of selected operating-system resources. The image supplies the workload's filesystem environment; it is not usually a complete separately booted kernel.

A virtual machine normally presents virtual hardware to a guest operating system with its own kernel. Several containers can run inside one virtual machine. Desktop container products may themselves use a virtual machine to provide the needed operating-system environment, so “containers share a kernel” does not mean every application directly uses the desktop's native kernel in every setup.

Isolation is valuable but not a magical security guarantee. Privileged settings, mounted host paths, vulnerable dependencies, excessive capabilities, and shared-kernel risks still matter. For this introductory lesson, the useful distinction is packaging and process isolation versus a whole guest-machine environment. You do not need to memorize low-level kernel APIs yet.

sections.title: Keep the artifact separate from its deployment settings
sections.markdown:
The same tested notes image might run in a local learning environment and a staging environment. Their database addresses, log levels, and allowed hostnames may differ. Supply appropriate configuration when starting the workload rather than rebuilding application logic for every environment.

Credentials require stronger handling than ordinary settings. Do not bake a database password into a reusable image or print it in startup logs. Inject access through the environment's controlled secret mechanism with appropriate permissions and rotation. A setting named secret is not automatically encrypted or protected; the platform's actual storage and access policy matters.

Network access also needs configuration. A process listening inside a container does not necessarily make it reachable from every external client. The runtime or platform must arrange the relevant network path, ports, and policy. Return to the addresses-and-proxies lessons: packaging the program does not replace DNS, routing, HTTPS, or authorization.

sections.title: Replacement is normal, so decide what must survive it
sections.markdown:
A container has a lifecycle. It can start, exit, be restarted, or be replaced with a new instance. Treat its private writable filesystem as unsuitable for the only copy of important user data unless you have deliberately provided durable storage with the required lifecycle. Temporary scratch files and caches have different needs from saved notes.

Suppose the notes app writes every new note inside its container, and a deployment replaces that container. The new instance starts from the image, not from a guaranteed copy of the old instance's private writes. Keeping user records in an external durable database makes replacement of the application process easier to reason about.

Databases can also run in containers. The important issue is not the word container; it is where their durable data lives, how it is attached, and which backup and recovery procedures have been tested. A persistent volume can preserve bytes across selected lifecycle events, but it does not automatically provide correct replication, disaster recovery, or freedom from accidental deletion.

sections.title: Kubernetes adds a manager for many running workloads
sections.markdown:
Running a few containers manually becomes awkward when machines fail, versions change, and several replicas need placement. Kubernetes is one platform that manages desired workloads across machines called nodes. It has a control plane that accepts configuration and makes management decisions, plus node components that run workloads.

The basic scheduled unit is a Pod. A Pod can contain one main application container or a few tightly related containers that need to share a lifecycle and network identity. Do not put every service into one Pod simply because they belong to the same product. Independently scalable responsibilities usually need independently manageable workloads.

A Deployment can express that the notes application should have three replicas from a particular Pod template. Controllers work to make observed state approach that desired state. If a Pod disappears, a replacement may be created; it is not the same immortal machine restored with all private memory. A separate Service provides stable discovery and traffic selection for appropriate backends, explained in the later networking chapter.

sections.title: Walk through a small deployment
sections.markdown:
Deploy a small note-title display change. Keep **artifact identity**, **traffic readiness**, and **business correctness** as separate checks.

~~~text
build identified image → test → start new instance → wait for readiness
                                               ↓
                     send limited traffic → verify save and read
                                               ↓
                         expand or stop → drain retired instance
~~~

Introduce the new instance while old healthy capacity still serves users. Confirm it can load required configuration and use its dependencies. Route a suitable share of traffic, then inspect errors, latency, and representative results before replacing more instances.

An old and new version overlap during a rolling update. Both must understand the data they encounter. A green startup probe does not prove that a new title belongs to the correct user's note.

When retiring an instance, stop new work and allow bounded time for active requests to finish or be handed off. The application must cooperate with termination signals and grace periods. A worker that acknowledges an unfinished job during shutdown can lose work even if the platform successfully starts its replacement.

sections.title: Application rollback cannot undo every data change
sections.markdown:
Imagine version 2 writes a new database format that version 1 cannot understand. If version 2 fails and you simply restart version 1, the old code may still fail on those new records. Deployment tooling can change which image runs; it cannot infer a correct reverse transformation for arbitrary business data.

Prefer compatible staged changes when possible. Add support for a new field while retaining old readers, migrate and validate data, switch writers carefully, and remove obsolete fields only after the compatibility window. That pattern is often called expand and contract. We will study live migrations in more depth later.

Check both application readiness and user outcomes during rollout. A process can answer its health endpoint while returning wrong note content. Keep a small representative verification path and observability that connects release version to failures. If the change affects an important invariant, run a concurrency or recovery scenario that actually tests it.

sections.title: Keep the layers in the right order
sections.markdown:
Explain the chain in your own words: source code becomes a built image; a runtime starts a container from it; Kubernetes can place that container inside a Pod and maintain desired replicas; network services direct requests to ready application instances; durable data stays in an explicitly managed store.

None of these layers proves the next layer's guarantee. A reproducible image does not mean the application is bug-free. A running Pod does not mean it is ready. Three replicas on one failing host may share a failure domain. An available database endpoint does not mean every query preserves your business invariant.

For general system-design practice, you should be able to describe how an application is packaged, replaced, and kept separate from its durable data. Deep Kubernetes configuration and provider-specific deployment products are optional extensions until the basic lifecycle makes sense. The later platform chapters will connect these terms to a real request path and operational controls.

diagrams.title: Replace the process while retaining the saved record
diagrams.source:
flowchart LR
I[Image digest D12] --> A[Old container A]
I --> B[Replacement container B]
A -->|Commit note n61| DB[(Durable database)]
B -->|Read note n61| DB
A -.-> X[Private memory disappears on replacement]
diagrams.caption: Both instances start from the same artifact. Persistent data survives only according to the separately configured storage guarantees; the image does not restore private memory.
steps: Identify the image used to start each instance.
Commit durable user data outside the replaceable process state.
Allow the replacement to reconnect to the intended data store.
Expect private memory and unpreserved scratch state to be absent.

D[Deployment desired state] -.->|Controller reconciles| P1[Ready Pod A]
D -.->|Controller reconciles| P2[Ready Pod B]
U[User request] --> S[Service and entry traffic path]
S --> P1

P1 --> DB[(Durable database)]
P2 --> DB
diagrams.caption: Dotted arrows are management relationships. User requests do not pass through the Deployment controller.
steps: Declare the desired application version and replica count.
The traffic path selects ready application backends.
Pods access durable data through the application’s normal storage protocol.

exercise.prompt: Explain what happens to an unsaved in-memory note and a committed database note when the application container is replaced. Then draw source→image→registry→running Pod, keeping management arrows separate from the user request. Name one condition that can make rollback unsafe.
rubric: Private memory is not recovered automatically by starting the same image.
Committed data follows the database’s durability guarantees.
The controller manages Pods rather than forwarding user HTTP traffic.
A backward-incompatible data change can break the older application.
exercise.solution: The new instance starts fresh process state, so an in-memory note with no durable save is not automatically restored. A committed note in the separately managed database remains subject to that database’s storage and failure guarantees. Build and distribute an image, then let the runtime/platform start it in a Pod. Draw the user path through the entry/Service to the application, and a separate dotted management arrow from the controller. Rollback may be unsafe if the new version wrote data the old code cannot interpret, even when restoring the old image succeeds.

questions.prompt: Two containers started from one image automatically share application memory.
questions.explanation: They are independent running instances; shared application state needs an explicit design.

questions.explanation: Old code may not understand newly written data or schema semantics.

questions.prompt: What does Kubernetes add beyond an individual container runtime?
questions.answer: It manages desired workloads across nodes, including placement and controller-driven lifecycle, while the runtime executes containers. Application correctness and durable storage still require explicit design.
questions.explanation: It manages desired workloads across nodes, including placement and controller-driven lifecycle, while the runtime executes containers. Application correctness and durable storage still require explicit design.

questions.prompt: Why is a Pod being Running not sufficient proof of a healthy user experience?
questions.answer: Its process may not be ready for requests, dependencies may fail, or its business logic may return incorrect results. Readiness and representative user-outcome checks answer different questions.
questions.explanation: Its process may not be ready for requests, dependencies may fail, or its business logic may return incorrect results. Readiness and representative user-outcome checks answer different questions.

flashcards.back: A running program with execution state and memory.
A packaged starting artifact versus a running workload instance.
Containers usually share a kernel; a typical VM has a guest kernel behind virtualized hardware.
No. Durable application state needs an explicit persistent design.
Identified artifact, readiness, compatible overlap, observed user outcomes, and a valid recovery plan.

mentalModel: Package the application reproducibly, run it as replaceable instances, and make persistence and rollout safety explicit.

walkthroughs.title: What actually moves to the replacement?
walkthroughs.intro: An application replacement uses the same image digest D12 and database. This example assumes that database remains available and durable.

steps.title: Start A
steps.explanation: Instance A starts from the image and connects to the notes database.

steps.title: Change two kinds of state
steps.explanation: A user commits n62. A temporary progress counter remains only in A’s memory.

steps.title: Replace A with B
steps.explanation: B starts with fresh private memory. Neither reusing the digest nor the container name transfers A’s variables.

steps.title: Verify the user journey
steps.explanation: Read n62 through B, then perform a small permitted save. These checks test more than whether B has a running process.

state.label: Limit
state.value: No claim of recovery if the database also failed

walkthroughs.takeaway: The image recreates the program environment. The data design recreates access to durable user state.
